sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Distributed tracing is the practice of recording a single user request's path across multiple services as a tree of spans — each span representing one service's work on the request, all sharing a trace ID — so that operators can reconstruct the request's flow, measure each service's latency contribution, and pinpoint the slow or failing service in a microservices system where a single request may touch dozens of services.

In a monolith, a slow request is easy to debug: you turn on logging, reproduce the request, and the logs show which function was slow. In a microservices system, a single user request fans out across many services — the API gateway calls the order service, which calls inventory, payment, and shipping, which call their own downstreams — and a slow request might be slow because of any one of them. Per-service logs do not help, because you cannot easily tell which log lines across which services belong to the same request. Without distributed tracing, debugging a slow microservices request is a forensic nightmare: you correlate timestamps across services, guess at causal chains, and often conclude "we think it was the inventory service, but we're not sure." Distributed tracing solves this by tagging every request with a trace ID at the ingress, propagating that ID through every service hop via headers, and recording a span for each service's work — the span includes the service name, operation name, start time, duration, and the parent span ID. The result is a tree of spans (the trace) that shows the entire request's flow, with per-service latency breakdown, so the operator can see at a glance which service was slow.

The trace IDs and span IDs are the foundation. A **trace ID** is a globally unique identifier for the end-to-end request (typically a 128-bit hex string), assigned at the ingress (the API gateway or the first service that sees the request). A **span ID** is a unique identifier for one service's work on the request (typically a 64-bit hex string), generated by each service when it starts its span. A **parent span ID** links a child span to its caller's span, forming the trace tree. When service A calls service B, A's tracing library injects the trace ID, A's span ID (as the parent), and a new span ID for B into the request headers (typically `traceparent` / `tracestate` in W3C Trace Context, or `X-B3-TraceId` / `X-B3-SpanId` / `X-B3-ParentSpanId` in B3). B's tracing library extracts these, starts a child span with A's span as parent, does its work, and propagates the trace ID to its own downstream calls. The spans are emitted (via background batching, to avoid blocking the request) to a tracing backend — Jaeger, Zipkin, Tempo, Datadog, or AWS X-Ray — which assembles them into a trace tree and provides a UI to explore it.

The real-world journey that made distributed tracing mainstream was Uber's. In 2015–2016, Uber had hundreds of microservices, and a single user request (e.g., requesting a ride) touched 50+ services. When a request was slow, the on-call engineer spent hours correlating logs across services, often failing to identify the culprit. Uber initially adopted Twitter's Zipkin (open-sourced in 2012, based on Google's Dapper paper), but found it could not scale to Uber's volume, so they built Jaeger (open-sourced in 2017, now a CNCF graduated project). With Jaeger, an on-call engineer could open a slow request's trace and see, in seconds, that the surge-pricing service took 800 ms of the request's 1.2 s — the diagnosis went from hours to seconds. Twitter had the same journey with Zipkin: their microservices made per-service logs insufficient, and Zipkin (named after the street name of Twitter's old office, Zipkin Street) gave them the trace tree that made slow requests debuggable. Google's Dapper (2010 paper) was the academic foundation: it formalized the trace/span model, the propagation mechanism, and the sampling strategies that all modern tracing systems use.

The sampling strategy is critical because tracing every request is too expensive at scale. A service handling 100,000 req/s, emitting a span per request with 200 bytes per span, generates 20 MB/s of trace data — far too much to store or process. Sampling selects a subset of requests to trace. **Head-based sampling**: the ingress decides at request time whether to trace (e.g., 1% of requests, random), and propagates the "trace this" decision via headers. This is cheap and uniform, but it misses rare errors (a 1% sample may not capture a 0.1% error rate). **Tail-based sampling**: every request is traced in memory, and at the end of the request a sampling decision is made based on the request's characteristics (e.g., trace all errors, all slow requests, and 1% of normal requests). Tail-based sampling captures interesting requests (errors, slowness) at much lower volume, but it requires holding the trace in memory until completion, which is more expensive. Modern systems use a combination: head-based for routine traffic, tail-based for errors and outliers. OpenTelemetry's Collector supports both, with configurable policies.

The trade-offs of distributed tracing are real. **Instrumentation cost**: every service must have the tracing library integrated, and every downstream call must propagate the trace headers — missing propagation breaks the trace tree, making the trace useless. **Performance overhead**: even with sampling, the tracing library adds CPU (header injection/extraction, span generation, batching) and memory (span buffers). **Storage cost**: trace data is voluminous even at 1% sampling, and retention is a balance (7–30 days is typical). **Operational complexity**: the tracing backend (Jaeger, Zipkin) is a distributed system to operate, with its own storage (Cassandra, Elasticsearch) and scaling concerns. **Adoption friction**: getting every team to instrument every service is a multi-quarter effort, and missing instrumentation breaks traces. The standardization of OpenTelemetry (a CNCF project that merged OpenTracing and OpenCensus in 2019) has reduced this friction — one library, one API, multiple backend exporters — but adoption is still non-trivial.

The deeper lesson is that distributed tracing is not just a debugging tool; it is the primary observability signal for microservices systems. Metrics tell you that something is wrong (error rate spiked); logs tell you what happened in one service; traces tell you where in the request flow it happened and which services were involved. Without traces, the operator knows "the system is slow" but not "the surge-pricing service is slow." With traces, the diagnosis is immediate, and the on-call engineer can fix the actual problem rather than guessing. For any microservices system above ~10 services, distributed tracing is as essential as metrics and logs — the three pillars of observability. The investment in OpenTelemetry instrumentation pays off across the system's lifetime, in faster incident response, better capacity planning, and clearer understanding of service dependencies.

sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Gateway as API Gateway
    participant Order as Order Service
    participant Inv as Inventory
    participant Pay as Payment
    participant Ship as Shipping

    Client->>Gateway: GET /checkout (trace_id=T1, span=S1)
    Note over Gateway: span S1 starts (parent=root)
    Gateway->>Order: POST /order (trace_id=T1, parent=S1, span=S2)
    Note over Order: span S2 starts (parent=S1)
    Order->>Inv: GET /stock (trace_id=T1, parent=S2, span=S3)
    Note over Inv: span S3 starts (parent=S2) - takes 800ms
    Inv-->>Order: 200 OK
    Order->>Pay: POST /charge (trace_id=T1, parent=S2, span=S4)
    Note over Pay: span S4 starts (parent=S2)
    Pay-->>Order: 200 OK
    Order->>Ship: POST /schedule (trace_id=T1, parent=S2, span=S5)
    Note over Ship: span S5 starts (parent=S2)
    Ship-->>Order: 200 OK
    Order-->>Gateway: 200 OK
    Gateway-->>Client: 200 OK
    Note over Gateway,Ship: All spans (S1-S5) share trace_id=T1, sent to Jaeger
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
   client request: GET /checkout
        |
        v
   +-----------+  trace_id=T1, span=S1 (root, gateway)
   | gateway   |  duration: 1200ms
   +-----+-----+
         |  propagate: traceparent: 00-T1-S1-01
         v
   +-----------+  span=S2 (order, parent=S1)
   | order svc |  duration: 1100ms
   +--+--+--+--+
      |  |  |   parallel calls (or sequential):
      |  |  |
      |  |  +---> +-----------+  span=S5 (shipping, parent=S2) dur:50ms
      |  |        | shipping  |  -> 200 OK
      |  |        +-----------+
      |  |
      |  +------> +-----------+  span=S4 (payment, parent=S2) dur:200ms
      |           | payment   |  -> 200 OK
      |           +-----------+
      |
      +---------> +-----------+  span=S3 (inventory, parent=S2) dur:800ms  <-- SLOW!
                 | inventory |  -> 200 OK
                 +-----------+

   trace tree (assembled in Jaeger):
   T1 (root, gateway, 1200ms)
   |- S2 (order, 1100ms)
      |- S3 (inventory, 800ms)   <-- bottleneck, ~67% of total
      |- S4 (payment, 200ms)
      |- S5 (shipping, 50ms)

   diagnosis: inventory is the slow service (800ms vs expected 50ms)
```

### Walkthrough
1. The client request arrives at the API gateway, which assigns a trace ID (T1) and starts the root span (S1). The tracing library (OpenTelemetry) records the span's start time and propagates the trace ID, span ID, and parent ID via headers (`traceparent: 00-T1-S1-01`) on every downstream call.
2. Each downstream service extracts the headers, starts a child span (with the caller's span as parent), does its work, and propagates the trace ID to its own downstream calls. Inventory's span (S3) takes 800 ms; payment (S4) takes 200 ms; shipping (S5) takes 50 ms. Each span is emitted (in background batches) to the tracing backend (Jaeger) with its service name, operation, start time, duration, and parent ID.
3. The tracing backend assembles the spans into a trace tree (all spans sharing trace ID T1) and provides a UI. The operator opens the trace and sees the tree: gateway 1200 ms -> order 1100 ms -> inventory 800 ms (the bottleneck, ~67% of total). The diagnosis that took hours with log correlation now takes seconds — the operator knows inventory is the slow service and can investigate it directly, rather than guessing across services.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Distributed tracing mock: trace ID + span ID propagation across services.
- Demonstrates how a single request's flow is recorded as a tree of spans,
- Assembled by a tracing backend (Jaeger/Zipkin) for diagnosis.
- Tracing backend (mock Jaeger/Zipkin)
- Tracer: each service uses this to start spans + propagate IDs
- W3C traceparent format: 00-{trace_id}-{span_id}-01
- Mock services that propagate the trace
- Call order service, propagating trace headers.

**Defines:** `TracingBackend`, `Tracer`, `Span`, `gateway()`, `order_service()`, `inventory_service()`, `payment_service()`, `shipping_service()`

```python
# Distributed tracing mock: trace ID + span ID propagation across services.
# Demonstrates how a single request's flow is recorded as a tree of spans,
# assembled by a tracing backend (Jaeger/Zipkin) for diagnosis.

import uuid, time, random
from collections import defaultdict

# ---- Tracing backend (mock Jaeger/Zipkin) ----
class TracingBackend:
    def __init__(self):
        self.spans = []  # list of span dicts

    def emit(self, span):
        self.spans.append(span)

    def show_trace(self, trace_id):
        spans = [s for s in self.spans if s["trace_id"] == trace_id]
        by_id = {s["span_id"]: s for s in spans}
        roots = [s for s in spans if s["parent_id"] is None]
        print(f"\n=== Trace {trace_id[:12]} ({len(spans)} spans) ===")
        def render(span, depth=0):
            indent = "  " * depth
            print(f"{indent}- {span['service']}.{span['op']}  "
                  f"duration={span['duration_ms']:.0f}ms  "
                  f"span={span['span_id'][:8]}")
            for s in spans:
                if s["parent_id"] == span["span_id"]:
                    render(s, depth + 1)
        for r in roots:
            render(r)

backend = TracingBackend()

# ---- Tracer: each service uses this to start spans + propagate IDs ----
class Tracer:
    def __init__(self, service):
        self.service = service

    def start_span(self, op, trace_id=None, parent_id=None):
        span_id = uuid.uuid4().hex
        if trace_id is None:
            trace_id = uuid.uuid4().hex  # new trace at ingress
        return Span(self.service, op, trace_id, span_id, parent_id)

class Span:
    def __init__(self, service, op, trace_id, span_id, parent_id):
        self.service, self.op = service, op
        self.trace_id, self.span_id, self.parent_id = trace_id, span_id, parent_id
        self.start = time.time()
        self.duration_ms = None

    def __enter__(self):
        return self

    def __exit__(self, *a):
        self.duration_ms = (time.time() - self.start) * 1000
        backend.emit({
            "service": self.service, "op": self.op,
            "trace_id": self.trace_id, "span_id": self.span_id,
            "parent_id": self.parent_id, "duration_ms": self.duration_ms,
        })

    def headers(self):
        # W3C traceparent format: 00-{trace_id}-{span_id}-01
        return {"traceparent": f"00-{self.trace_id}-{self.span_id}-01"}

# ---- Mock services that propagate the trace ----
def gateway():
    tracer = Tracer("gateway")
    with tracer.start_span("GET /checkout") as span:
        # Call order service, propagating trace headers.
        order_service(headers=span.headers(), parent_span=span)

def order_service(headers, parent_span):
    tracer = Tracer("order")
    # Extract trace_id and parent_id from incoming headers.
    tp = headers["traceparent"].split("-")
    trace_id, parent_id = tp[1], tp[2]
    with tracer.start_span("POST /order", trace_id, parent_id) as span:
        # Fan out to inventory (slow!), payment, shipping.
        inventory_service(span.headers(), span)
        payment_service(span.headers(), span)
        shipping_service(span.headers(), span)

def inventory_service(headers, parent_span):
    tracer = Tracer("inventory")
    trace_id, parent_id = headers["traceparent"].split("-")[1:3]
    with tracer.start_span("GET /stock", trace_id, parent_id):
        time.sleep(0.8)  # <-- the slow service

def payment_service(headers, parent_span):
    tracer = Tracer("payment")
    trace_id, parent_id = headers["traceparent"].split("-")[1:3]
    with tracer.start_span("POST /charge", trace_id, parent_id):
        time.sleep(0.2)

def shipping_service(headers, parent_span):
    tracer = Tracer("shipping")
    trace_id, parent_id = headers["traceparent"].split("-")[1:3]
    with tracer.start_span("POST /schedule", trace_id, parent_id):
        time.sleep(0.05)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    t0 = time.time()
    gateway()
    # Show the trace tree from the backend.
    trace_id = backend.spans[0]["trace_id"]
    backend.show_trace(trace_id)
    print(f"\ntotal wall clock: {time.time()-t0:.2f}s")
```
